summary:
Luna Base: 30 Days is an isometric pixel-art lunar base management game designed for junior astronauts. Players run a Moon outpost at Shackleton Ridge for 30 mission days, balancing power, water, food, air and the wellbeing of a four-person crew (Maya, Leo, Sam and Aria).

Each day, players plan how to use the base. They switch power to rooms, assign astronauts to jobs, and build or upgrade from 12 room types, including a Water Recycling Facility, Greenhouse, Power Station, Life Support Room, Medical Bay, Research Laboratory, Engineering Workshop and Radiation Shelter. Sunlight levels, eclipses, equipment damage and radiation warnings then shape how the day plays out. Players respond with seven short mini-games, such as repairing micrometeorite damage, sweeping dust off solar arrays, solving a water pipe puzzle, bracing against moonquakes, and deflecting solar particles.

The game is grounded in real space science. Thirteen science cards connect each system to NASA sources, including ISS water recovery (98%), the DONKI space weather database, Artemis sunlight at the lunar south pole, ISS plant growth experiments and in-space 3D printing. Every card is labeled as an archived NASA observation, a simplified game value, or fiction, so players know what is real. By the end, players understand why every drop of water, watt of power and crew member matters on the Moon.
details:
What it does and how it works: Luna Base: 30 Days is a browser-based, isometric pixel-art management game set at Shackleton Ridge on the Moon. Over 30 mission days, players plan each day by powering rooms, assigning four astronauts to jobs, and building or upgrading 12 room types. A simulation engine then plays out the day using sunlight levels, eclipses, equipment wear and random events. Players step in with seven short mini-games: solar deflection, dust sweeping, a water pipe puzzle, micrometeorite repair, moonquake bracing, triage monitoring and extreme-cold energy management. A final report scores the mission.

Benefits and intended impact: Young learners experience why every drop of water, watt of power and crew member matters in space. The aim is to build curiosity about space exploration and an understanding of how real life-support systems work.

Use of NASA and space data: Thirteen in-game science cards link game systems to real sources. These include ISS water recovery (98%), the DONKI space weather database, Artemis sunlight at the lunar south pole, ISS plant growth research, in-space 3D printing and VIPER water ice findings. Each card is labeled as an archived NASA observation, a simplified game value, or fiction, so players know what is real.

Tools and technology: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, a custom HTML canvas isometric renderer, Motion for animation, Lucide icons and a built-in sound engine. The project was built and remixed in Google AI Studio.

Creativity: The game turns life-support science into a story-driven puzzle experience. It combines base-building, minigames and playful story events, such as a clearly fictional rival visitor that players can skip.

Factors considered: Age-appropriate difficulty, a simple rule of one food and one water per astronaut per day, honest labeling of simplified science, and touch and mouse controls.
